historical_timeline.summary: Born in Los Angeles; grows up in Watts.
Olympic silver medal in the 200 meters, Los Angeles.
World records at 100 and 200 meters; three Olympic gold medals and a silver in Seoul.
Treated for seizures in 1990, 1993 and 1994, as later reported from the coroner's records.
Co-chair of the President's Council on Physical Fitness and Sports.
Inducted into the U.S. Track and Field Hall of Fame.
Seizure on a flight to St. Louis; discharged from hospital the next day.
Dies in her sleep at home in Mission Viejo, California, at 38; the coroner reports positional asphyxia during an epileptic seizure caused by a cavernous angioma.

claims.statement: Florence Griffith was born in Los Angeles on December 21, 1959, the seventh of eleven children, and grew up from the age of four in a public housing project in the Watts neighborhood of Los Angeles. Reference works give her given names in both orders, Delorez Florence and Florence Delorez.

claims.statement: She ran for California State University, Northridge, and then for UCLA, graduating in 1983, and won the silver medal in the 200 meters at the 1984 Olympic Games in Los Angeles, competing as Florence Griffith.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Anchors the modern social history of an elite sprinter.

source_links.locator: CSUN; UCLA 1983; 1984 silver in the 200 meters

claims.statement: In 1988 she set a world record of 10.49 seconds for 100 meters at the U.S. Olympic Trials and, at the Seoul Olympic Games, won gold medals in the 100 meters, the 200 meters (in a world record of 21.34 seconds) and the 4 x 100 meters relay, and a silver medal in the 4 x 400 meters relay. She retired from competition in 1989.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Her athletic career anchors the modern goal of returning to training.

claims.statement: In April 1996 she had a seizure on an airplane on the way to St. Louis. She was taken to hospital and discharged the next day, and her family asked that no other details be released.

claims.statement: She died in her sleep at her home in Mission Viejo, California, on September 21, 1998, at 38. The Orange County Sheriff-Coroner reported that she died of positional asphyxia during an epileptic seizure, and that the seizure was caused by a congenital cavernous angioma (cavernous malformation) of the left orbital frontal cerebrum.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The documented disease to which the synthetic diagnosis is linked. History only, stated without detail.

synthetic_episode.teaching_objective: Evaluate an adult after a generalized seizure as the AAN/AES first unprovoked seizure guideline directs: history, examination and laboratory screen, EEG, and MRI of the brain with susceptibility-weighted imaging, which here shows a cavernous malformation; diagnose epilepsy after a single unprovoked seizure when an epileptogenic lesion makes recurrence likely (ILAE 2014 practical definition); choose an antiseizure medication for a woman who could become pregnant (levetiracetam or lamotrigine, with folic acid, contraception counseling and the reasons to avoid valproate, under the AAN/AES/SMFM 2024 guideline); refer for neurosurgical evaluation of an epileptogenic cavernous malformation and consider lesionectomy (Angioma Alliance 2017); tell her about SUDEP and how to lower the risk, as the AAN/AES 2017 guideline requires; give seizure safety advice for driving under California law, water and sleep, with nocturnal seizure detection; and plan a safe return to elite-level training.

hpi.narrative: Ms. Griffith Joyner returns two weeks after her first visit. The sleep-deprived EEG two days after that visit showed intermittent left frontal sharp waves and slowing. MRI of the brain six days after the visit, with susceptibility-weighted imaging, shows a single 1.4 cm cavernous malformation in the left orbitofrontal cortex with a hemosiderin rim and an adjacent developmental venous anomaly, and no other lesion. Dr. Mehta-Sorensen of the epilepsy service saw her this morning. She has had no further seizure, spell or headache. She has not driven, showers rather than bathes, and has not swum. The records of her earlier seizure care have been requested and have not arrived. She is not pregnant (negative test at the first visit) and is not planning a pregnancy now. She has had no thoughts of self-harm.

assessment_plan.display: Focal epilepsy with structural cause from a left orbitofrontal cavernous malformation
assessment_plan.assessment: The seizure was a focal to bilateral tonic-clonic seizure arising from the left orbitofrontal cortex, where the EEG shows epileptiform discharges and the MRI shows a cavernous malformation. Under the ILAE 2014 practical definition this is epilepsy after a single unprovoked seizure, because an epileptogenic lesion with matching EEG discharges carries a recurrence risk above 60%; her earlier seizures by history point the same way. Dr. Mehta-Sorensen recommends an antiseizure medication now and a neurosurgical opinion on lesionectomy. Levetiracetam is chosen for a woman who could become pregnant: low risk of birth defects, no interaction with hormonal contraception, and an effective dose from the first day; lamotrigine would need weeks of slow titration and its level falls with estrogen-containing contraception. Valproate is avoided because it carries the highest risk of major malformations and of lower intelligence in children exposed in pregnancy. Folic acid 0.4 mg daily. Levetiracetam can cause irritability or low mood, so mood is checked at each visit; baseline PHQ-9 is 3

hpi.narrative: Ms. Griffith Joyner returns three weeks after starting levetiracetam. She has taken every dose. In the first ten days she felt short-tempered and more tired than usual after training; both are easing. She has had no seizure or spell. The neurosurgeon saw her last week and offered complete removal of the cavernous malformation with its hemosiderin rim through a left frontal craniotomy; she has chosen surgery, booked in three weeks. She wears the detection watch at night. She has not driven. She has had no thoughts of self-harm.

hpi.narrative: Ms. Griffith Joyner returns five weeks after a left frontal craniotomy with complete removal of the cavernous malformation and its hemosiderin rim. She went home on the third day. The MRI the day after surgery showed complete resection. She needed acetaminophen for about two weeks and nothing since. The incision has healed. She has had no seizure, spell, headache, or change in smell, mood or concentration. She has walked daily since the second week and began easy running last week without symptoms. She takes levetiracetam twice a day; the irritability has gone. She has not driven. She has had no thoughts of self-harm.

consultant_note.history: Ms. Griffith Joyner, 36, is seen at the request of Dr. Vanterpool two weeks after her first visit for a generalized tonic-clonic seizure on a flight. Others described stiffening and then jerking of all four limbs with confusion afterwards; she remembers nothing of it. She has had treatment for seizures elsewhere in the past, and those records have not arrived. There was no provoking factor. She has had no seizure since. She trains most days, flies often for work, and has stopped driving. She is not pregnant and is not planning a pregnancy now. She wants the details kept private
consultant_note.data_reviewed: Dr. Vanterpool's intake note and laboratory results: blood count, electrolytes, glucose, calcium, magnesium, creatinine, ALT and creatine kinase normal; pregnancy test negative. Sleep-deprived EEG: intermittent left frontal sharp waves and focal slowing, maximal at F7 and Fp1; no generalized discharges. MRI of the brain, epilepsy protocol with susceptibility-weighted imaging and gadolinium: a 1.4 cm cavernous malformation in the left orbitofrontal cortex with a complete hemosiderin rim (Zabramski type II), an adjacent developmental venous anomaly, no other lesion, and no acute hemorrhage

exam.finding: Fit and well; weight 61.2 kg; blood pressure 110/68, pulse 58
Alert and oriented; smell intact in each nostril; cranial nerves, strength, reflexes, sensation, coordination and gait normal

assessment.assessment: The seizure was focal in onset, from the left orbitofrontal cortex, and spread to both hemispheres (focal to bilateral tonic-clonic). The EEG discharges match the site of the cavernous malformation. Under the ILAE 2014 practical definition, one unprovoked seizure with an epileptogenic lesion and matching discharges is epilepsy, because the risk of another seizure exceeds 60%; her earlier seizures add to that. I recommend starting an antiseizure medication now. For a woman who could become pregnant, levetiracetam or lamotrigine carries the lowest risk of birth defects; levetiracetam reaches an effective dose at once and does not interact with hormonal contraception, while lamotrigine needs about six weeks of titration and its level falls with estrogen. Valproate should be avoided. Levetiracetam can cause irritability or low mood, which should be asked about at each visit. She should take folic acid 0.4 mg daily and plan any pregnancy with the epilepsy team. SUDEP should be discussed with her at diagnosis; today's visit did not allow a full discussion, so I have asked that it be the first item at her next primary care visit: SUDEP is uncommon but real, tonic-clonic seizures are the main risk, and freedom from them is the best protection

assessment.display: Solitary cerebral cavernous malformation, left orbitofrontal
assessment.assessment: A single cavernous malformation with a developmental venous anomaly is the sporadic form, so familial genetic testing is not needed. Because it is the source of her epilepsy and lies in accessible cortex, neurosurgical evaluation is recommended: complete removal with the surrounding hemosiderin rim gives a high chance of freedom from seizures, and early surgery is associated with better seizure outcomes than surgery after years of seizures

recommendations: Levetiracetam 500 mg twice daily from today, with mood and irritability checked at each visit; switch to lamotrigine if mood effects are troublesome; avoid valproate
Folic acid 0.4 mg daily; contraception and pregnancy planning reviewed at each visit
Neurosurgical evaluation within three weeks for lesionectomy of the cavernous malformation with its hemosiderin rim; continue levetiracetam through and for at least two years after surgery
Seizure diary, written seizure action plan, and emergency services for a seizure lasting five minutes or more
SUDEP counseling as the first item at the next primary care visit, with nocturnal supervision or a wrist-worn seizure detection device
Safety: showers instead of baths, swimming only with a companion who knows first aid, no heights or working alone near water; flying is allowed with medication in hand luggage
Driving only when the California DMV clears her after review of her seizure control; return to training on a graded plan after any surgery
Report sudden severe headache or new neurological symptoms at once, which could mean bleeding from the malformation
